specPoints.text: practical: investigate the conditions needed for seed germination

primer.text: Why does a seed sprout in damp warm soil but sit dormant in a dry freezer? This practical answers it with four test tubes: each tube removes exactly one condition — water, oxygen or warmth — while tube B keeps everything. The pattern of sprouting, read against the CORMS design rules, isolates what germination truly needs.

lessons.title: Three Conditions, Four Tubes
lessons.opening: Germination needs three conditions — water to swell the seed and activate enzymes, oxygen for respiration, and warmth for enzyme activity — and the four-tube design removes each one in turn so only the complete control tube germinates.
keyPoints: Water swells a seed so its coat splits open, waking the enzymes that run growth.
Oxygen is necessary for respiration to provide energy.
Warmth increases enzyme activity until a certain temperature.
Tube A lacks water, tube C is sealed under water and oil so oxygen is blocked, and tube D sits in a fridge without warmth.
Tube B is the control with every condition present.

low.restatement: Water, oxygen and warmth are the trio; knock out any one of them and the seeds stay dormant.
low.analogy: A fire needing fuel, air and a spark: remove one ingredient and nothing burns.
low.examPointer: Pair each tube with the missing condition — A water, C oxygen, D warmth, B control.

medium.restatement: The design isolates variables: oil floating on tube C's water layer shuts out the oxygen while still soaking the seeds, and the fridge in tube D removes warmth without touching water, so any germination difference traces cleanly to the single factor removed.
medium.analogy: Three locked rooms with one light switched off in each, revealing which switch the bulb actually needs.
medium.examPointer: When asked why tube C is not just 'wet', mention the oil layer blocking oxygen — that detail is the discriminator.

check.stem: Which three conditions does a seed need for germination?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
None of these is a taught germination condition.
Carbon dioxide is not needed before photosynthesis starts.
Soil and fertiliser are not required for germination itself.

check.stem: Why does water help germination begin?

options.text: It swells the seed until the coat splits and the growth enzymes wake
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It feeds the seedling glucose directly
options.explanation: Water carries no glucose; the seed digests its own store.
The seed leaves are not dissolved.

options.text: It supplies oxygen to the embryo
options.explanation: Oxygen enters as a gas, not inside water.

check.stem: In tube C, seeds sit under water covered by a layer of oil. Which condition has been removed?

options.text: Oxygen, blocked by the water and oil layers
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Tube C stays at room temperature.
Tube C is soaked — water is abundant there.
Oil does not destroy the seed's enzymes.

check.stem: What role does the control tube play in this design?

options.text: The control, with all three conditions present for comparison
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Tube C tests oxygen removal.
Tube D tests warmth removal.
Tube A removes water; tube B removes nothing.

check.stem: Which result would falsify the claim that all three conditions are needed?

options.text: Seeds germinating fully in tube A, C or D
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That confirms the claim.
D germinating would falsify warmth's need, but B alone is expected — the falsifier is any removed-condition tube sprouting.
That suggests setup failure, not a condition refutation.

check.stem: State what water does to the seed when germination starts.
check.modelAnswer: Water swells the seed so the coat splits and the growth enzymes switch on.

check.stem: Name the condition each test tube removes or keeps.
check.modelAnswer: Tube A removes water, tube B is the control with all conditions, tube C blocks oxygen, and tube D removes warmth in the fridge.

check.stem: Explain why warmth improves germination up to a point.
check.modelAnswer: Warmth increases the activity of the enzymes that digest the seed's food store, so germination speeds up until higher temperatures start to denature them.

check.stem: A student sets up a fifth tube with moist cotton wool on a warm windowsill in bright light. Predict and explain the outcome.
check.modelAnswer: The seeds should germinate, because water, warmth and oxygen are all present, and light is not a required condition for germination.

lessons.title: Method, Results and the CORMS Design
lessons.opening: Ten cress seeds go onto cotton wool in each of four labelled tubes — A dry, B moist, C flooded with an oil layer, D moist and refrigerated — and after three to five days the germinated count is compared, with the CORMS prompt checking the design from change and organism to repeats, measures and sameness.
keyPoints: Each test tube holds 10 cress seeds on cotton wool, labelled A, B, C and D.
Tube A stays dry, tube B is moistened, tube C is covered with water plus an oil layer, and tube D is moistened and refrigerated.
Tubes A, B and C are kept at room temperature around 20 degrees.
From day 3 to day 5 the wool in tubes B and D must stay moist, and germinated seeds are counted.
CORMS covers the change, the organism, repeats, the measurement and the controlled sameness.

low.restatement: Set up four tubes of cress seeds, remove one condition from three of them, wait a few days and count sprouts.
low.analogy: Four identical puzzles with one piece hidden in each of three boxes.
low.examPointer: Quote the numbers: 10 seeds per tube, 3 to 5 days, room temperature for A to C, fridge at 4 degrees for D.

medium.restatement: Reliability comes from the CORMS discipline: same-species seeds to start identical, repeats to guard against a dud batch, a counted measure of germination after a fixed interval, and sterile water with matched temperatures so nothing but the tested factor moves.
medium.analogy: A fair race: same runners, same track, one lane altered per heat.
medium.examPointer: For the CORMS letters, attach one concrete action each — changing the conditions, same parent plant, repeats, counting germinated seeds after a set time, same temperature and sterile water.

check.stem: How many cress seeds are placed in each test tube?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Three is the day count window, not the seed count.
Four is the tube count, not the seed count.
The method uses 10 seeds per tube.

check.stem: Which tubes must stay moist through the 3 to 5 day observation window?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
A is deliberately dry and C is flooded, not merely moist.
Tube A must stay dry for its test.
Tube D is moistened too and must not dry out.

check.stem: In the CORMS design, what does the letter O stand for in this investigation?

options.text: The organism — cress seeds all taken from the same parent plant or species
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The oxygen level in each tube
options.explanation: Oxygen is the tested condition, not the letter O.
Observation is not what O encodes here.
Temperature sits under the S of CORMS.

check.stem: Why are the investigation repeats part of good design?

options.text: Repeating the investigation several times makes the results reliable
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Repeats do not change temperature.
The control stays in place.

options.text: Repeats change the organism each time
options.explanation: CORMS requires the same organism, not new ones.

check.stem: Which CORMS element covers keeping tubes A, B and C at the same room temperature and using sterile water throughout?

options.text: S — controlling the sameness of everything except the tested factor
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
C is the condition being changed, not the ones held fixed.
M is counting germinated seeds after a set time.
R is running the trial again, not holding conditions steady.

check.stem: State how long the seeds are left before comparing germination, and where tube D is kept.
check.modelAnswer: The comparison happens after 3 to 5 days, and tube D is kept in a fridge.

check.stem: State what is measured in each tube at the end of the practical.
check.modelAnswer: The number of germinated seeds in each test tube is compared.

check.stem: Explain why the seeds should all come from the same parent plant in this investigation.
check.modelAnswer: Seeds from one parent plant keep the organism consistent, so germination differences reflect the tested condition rather than genetic variation between seeds.

check.stem: A class finds three seeds sprouting in tube C after five days. Suggest one explanation and one improvement.
check.modelAnswer: The oil layer may have left an air pocket giving some seeds oxygen, so the class should repeat the trial, pressing the layer down to seal fully and recounting with fresh seeds.

glossary.definition: The beginning of seed growth, requiring water, oxygen and warmth.
Tube B, in which all three conditions for germination are present.
The design prompt: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same.
